title: Why British Homes Had an Outside Toilet Until Shockingly Recently
fullText: In 1961, a child in Manchester woke at 2:00 in the morning, pulled on a coat, and walked out into the freezing dark to use the toilet. A brick shed at the bottom of the backyard. This was a city, not a farm, and nobody who lived there thought it was strange. That year, nearly 7% of households in England and Wales had no indoor toilet at all. But the surprising part isn't that it lasted this long. It's that someone built it this way on purpose. And the reason why is stranger than you'd think. Now, if you grew up in the United States, you already have a picture in your head for this. The outhouse, the little wooden shack outback with the cresant moon on the door, the thing your greatgrandparents used on a farm in Kansas before the county ran water lines out to them. And you would be right to picture it because America had exactly that. As recently as the 1,950 census, about a quarter of all American homes had no complete indoor plumbing. And in rural areas, it was more than half. Go back to 1,940 and over a third of American homes had no flush toilet at all. In Mississippi that year, the number was close to 80%. So, the outhouse is not a British invention and it was never uniquely British. What happened next is where the two countries split. In America, the outhouse was mostly a rural story and it disappeared fast. People moved to cities and suburbs where water lines were cheap to install because everyone lived close together and a huge national push wired up the countryside. By the 2000 census, the share of American homes without indoor plumbing had dropped to 0.6%. The outhouse became a memory, a thing on a postcard, a joke about the olden days. Britain did the opposite. The British outside toilet belonged to the cities. It sat in the packed backyards of terrace houses in the biggest industrial cities on Earth. It was built into brand new homes on purpose and instead of vanishing quietly, it dug in and refused to leave for the better part of a century. To understand how that happened, you have to start with what these things actually were. Because the outside toilet was not one thing. It went through a grim evolution and each stage was worse than it sounds. At the bottom of the ladder was the privy, a wooden bench with a hole cut in it, sitting over a pit or a bucket inside a small brick or wooden shed in the yard. No flush, no water. You did your business and it sat there. To keep the smell and the flies down, people threw ash from the coal fire or a handful of dry earth down the hole after every use, which is where the polite name comes from, the earth closet. For light at night, you brought a candle because there was no electricity out there. And for toilet paper, there was no toilet paper. People cut old newspaper into squares, pushed a skewer through the corner and hung the wad on a nail with a piece of string, black and white print because color newsprint didn't really exist yet. That was the standard and it stayed the standard in a lot of these homes long after the rest of the world had moved on. The British have a hundred names for this shed and the names tell you how normal it was. In the Northeast, it was the Netti. In Scotland and parts of the north, it was the Lavy. Down south, it was the privy or just the outside lav. Different word in every town, which is what happens when a thing is so ordinary that every community grows its own slang for it. And living with one shaped your whole day, especially in winter. In summer, the walk to the bottom of the yard was almost pleasant. In January, it was a small ordeal. You went out into the cold and the dark, and the little brick shed had no heat and often no light beyond the candle you carried. Spiders moved in for the shelter and the pipes ran cold. In a hard frost, the water in the system could freeze solid, so the toilet simply stopped working until it thawed and people kept a kettle of hot water on hand to coax the pipes back to life. This is exactly why almost every home also kept a chamber pot under the bed, a china bowl with a handle that a lot of families called, with blunt northern humor, the gazund, because it goes under the bed. Nobody wanted to cross a frozen yard at 3:00 in the morning if a pot within arms reach would do the job. And in the morning, somebody had to carry it out and empty it. That was the daily rhythm of the thing year after year for the entire life of the house. Now, here is the question that hangs over the early version of all this. If the toilet is just a bucket or a pit in your yard, what happens when it fills up? Somebody has to empty it. And the answer to that question is one of the strangest jobs in the history of work. They were called the night soil men. Night soil was the polite term for human waste. And these men with their horses and their carts came around to empty the pits and the buckets and the underground brick tanks called cesspools. They did it at night and not for privacy or good manners. It was actually the law in a lot of places that the work could only be done in the hours of darkness because the stench of a cart loaded with the waste of an entire street was so unbearable that it could not be inflicted on people during the day. In the terrace streets, there was a small hatch in the back wall of the toilet that opened onto the rear alley so the night soil man could reach in from the alley and rake out the waste without ever entering the yard. That is how the whole system was designed. A hole in the wall, an alley, a cart, and a man doing the worst job in the city in the middle of the night. And the scale of it is genuinely hard to picture. By 1810, the city of London had somewhere around 200,000 cesspools for a population of about 1 million people. Pits of human waste sitting under yards and cellers and basement all over the city, all needing to be emptied by hand. When a city is small and farmland is close, this almost works. The waste got carted a short distance out of town and sold to farmers who spread it on their fields. And for centuries, there was an ugly kind of balance to the whole arrangement. Nothing was truly wasted. But that balance depended on the fields staying near the city, and London was not staying small. As the city sprawled outward, the farmland got pushed farther and farther away. The carts had to travel longer to dump their loads. The work got slower and more expensive, and the waste began backing up in those pits faster than anyone could haul it off. And this is where the outside toilet stops being a quirk and starts being a catastrophe. Because the thing that created the modern British terrace house and locked the toilet outside for generations was the industrial revolution. In the space of a few decades, people poured off the land and into the cities to work in the factories and the mills. Manchester, Leeds, Birmingham, Liverpool, the northern industrial towns. They exploded in size. And all of those people needed somewhere to live fast and cheap. So developers threw up terrorist housing at incredible speed. Row after row after row of narrow brick houses sharing sidewalls packed as [music] tightly onto the land as the builder could manage. Here is a detail that explains almost everything about why the toilet ended up where it did. Before the First World War, roughly 90% of all housing in Britain was rented. Almost nobody owned their home. That means the people building these houses were landlords and factory owners. And their incentive was simple. cramm in as many rent paying bodies as possible and spend as little as possible doing it. Quality was not the goal. Volume was the goal. The purest and most brutal version of this was a design called the backto back. Picture a normal terrace house. Then imagine a second house glued directly onto the back of it sharing that rear wall. So the house has a front wall and two shared sidewalls and a shared back wall. And that's it. One external wall. Light and air can only get in from the front. And crucially, a backtoback has no backyard because the back of your house is the back of somebody else's house. No yard means no space for your own outside toilet. So the residents of these places shared one toilet block, sometimes at the end of the street serving dozens of families. In the worst districts of Victorian [music] Britain, you could have something like a hundred houses sharing a single privy. A deep pit in a shared courtyard with seats built over it, used by hundreds of people, emptied whenever the night soilmen got around to it. The very worst version even had a name that sounds almost quaint until you learn what it meant. The privy midden. A midden is a heap of refues. And a privy mitten was exactly that. A large open pit that collected not just human waste, but the ash, the food scraps, and the general filth of everyone who used it. All of it left to rot until it was dug out. Sanitary inspectors of the day described these pits as wet, foul, and constantly overflowing with the content sometimes carried out by wheelbarrow and dumped in the street before anyone came to cart it away for good. You can guess what that did. Cramming that many people around a shared pit of waste with drinking water often coming from the same ground turned these districts into engines of disease. Cholola typhoid dissentry outbreaks tore through the workingclass neighborhoods and for a long time nobody understood why they kept coming back. The government did eventually act on the housing itself. The Public Health Act of 1,875 gave local councils the power to ban new backtobacks and it triggered a wave of new building rules, the bylaws that reshaped the ordinary terrace house from the ground up. And here is the reveal that catches most people offg guard. Under these new bylaws, every new terrace house was legally required to have its own toilet, not a shared block down the street, its own. So the outside toilet was not a case of the rules being ignored. It was the rules being followed. When the law demanded a private toilet for every home, builders answered by putting a small privy in each individual backyard, still with a hatch to the rear alley so the night soilman could reach it. In its day, that outside toilet in the yard was the modern, legal, upgraded answer to a public health crisis. These bylaw terraces went up by the hundreds of thousands across every industrial town. And they were built so solidly and in such numbers that as late as 2011, they still made up more than 15% of every home in the entire United Kingdom. But the law could force every house to have its own toilet. It could not on its own decide where that toilet went. And the reason it went out in the yard and stayed out in the yard comes down to a single mistaken idea lodged deep in the Victorian mind. The belief that put the toilet outside and kept it there. The Victorians thought disease was caused by bad air. They called it myasma. The theory was that illness came from foul smells, from the stink of rot and waste and stagnant water hanging in the air, and that if you breathe that bad air, you got sick. Now sit with that for a second because it is the psychological key to the whole thing. If you sincerely believe that smells carry death, then the single most dangerous thing you could possibly do is bring a toilet inside your house. Indoors, where you eat and sleep and where your children breathe all night. Under the myasma theory, an indoor toilet isn't a convenience. It's [music] a poison you've installed in your own bedroom. Here is the part that flips how you see the whole thing. In the Victorian mind, putting the toilet outside was a health measure, plain and simple. You put the source of the bad smell as far from the living space as you possibly could out at the bottom of the yard, downwind behind the coal shed. And this belief was baked right into the architecture in a way that is almost eerie once you see it. In the standard terrace house, the toilet was often built into the back wall of the scullery, the little rear kitchen. The plumbing was right there, sharing a wall with the house. And yet, there was deliberately no door connecting it to the inside. You could not reach the toilet from within your own home. To use it, you had to go out the back door and come at it from the yard. Even though it was physically attached to the building, builders did this on purpose to keep the smell out of the living areas. The toilet was built right against the kitchen wall, and you still had to walk outside in the weather to reach it. All because the fear demanded it. And this is where the story turns because the science that should have ended all of this arrived surprisingly early and it changed almost nothing at first. In 1854, a colera outbreak ripped through the Soho district of London. A physician named Jon Snow didn't buy the bad air explanation. He mapped every single death house by house and he noticed the cases clustered tightly around one particular public water pump on Broad Street. He argued that cholera was spreading through contaminated water, not foul air. And in a now famous move, he had the handle removed from the pump so people couldn't draw from it. He had in effect cracked the case. It was the water. It was always the water. The waste from the cesspools and the privies was leaking into the drinking supply and that was killing people, not the smell. You would think that would flip a switch overnight. It didn't. The bad air believers held on for years. What finally forced the issue wasn't a scientific paper. It was a summer. In 1858, London got a brutal heatwave and the river tempames, which by then was little more than an open sewer carrying the waste of millions, cooked in the sun until the smell was so overpowering that it shut down the government. Members of parliament sitting right next to the river literally could not function. Curtains soaked in chemicals were hung over the windows and it barely helped. They called it the great stink and nothing motivates a lawmaker quite like the problem arriving under his own nose. So Parliament finally approved a gigantic project led by an engineer named Joseph Basiljette to build a proper network of sewers under London and carry the waste away. It worked. It's one of the great feats of Victorian engineering and it saved countless lives. And here is a piece that makes the whole thing sting a little more. The wealthy did not wait around for any of this. Middle-class and upperass Victorian homes were getting proper indoor bathrooms decades before working families ever did. By the 1890s, a city like Liverpool had water closets in nearly all of its homes. In the same era, an industrial northern town like Rodale had them in only about 7.5% of households as late as 1,96. Same country, same decade, two completely different worlds. The indoor toilet arrived on a schedule set by wealth. So for millions of ordinary families, how soon the toilet came indoors had almost nothing to do with the calendar and almost everything to do with the class they were born into. But notice what actually changed and what didn't. The cities built sewers. The waste got carried away properly. The flush toilet, the water closet gradually replaced the horrible pit privy. What did not change was the location. Even as the plumbing modernized, even as the flush toilet arrived, it stayed [music] outside. The old fear of indoor smells had hardened into simple habit and simple building custom, and the toilet remained a fixture of the backyard. The technology moved indoors everywhere except the one room it mattered most. Now, this is usually the point where somebody brings up Thomas Crarapper, so let's deal with him because almost everything people believe about him is wrong. He was a real man born in 1836 near Doncaster in Yorkshire and he ran a genuinely successful plumbing and sanitary equipment business [music] in Chelsea in London. That part is true. But he did not invent the flush toilet. The flush toilet existed before he was born. And no, the slang word people giggle about does not come from his surname. It's a coincidence that has fooled people for over a century. Crarapper was a good salesman and a real manufacturer who helped make the flush toilet normal and respectable. He was not the genius who dreamed it up. His name stuck because it makes a better story than the truth does. And it has been repeated so many times that people simply assume it must be real. So by the early 1900s, the pieces for an indoor bathroom all existed. The plumbing worked. The sewers worked. The germ theory of disease had won. And educated people knew perfectly well that a properly plumbed toilet indoors was not going to poison the air. The technology was ready. So why did millions of British homes keep the toilet outside for another 60, 70, even 80 years? Why did a British kid in 1961 still have to walk out into the frost in the middle of the night? The answer is a stack of very human reasons. And the first one is cold hard money. Remember, most people rented and the landlord owned the building. Moving a toilet indoors or adding a whole new indoor bathroom meant tearing into a solid brick house, running new pipes, sacrificing a bedroom or a storage cupboard and paying builders to do it. For a landlord, collecting rent on a cheap terrace, there was no reason to spend that money. The outside toilet worked. It flushed. The tenants weren't leaving over it. and the drains, the whole waste system already ran out the back of the house to that exact spot. The path of lease resistance and lease cost was to leave everything precisely where it was, so it stayed. Multiply that decision across millions of rented houses and dozens of decades, and you get a country that modernized almost everything about daily life while leaving the toilet stubbornly, permanently out in the cold. If you're finding this as strange and fascinating as I do, take a second to subscribe because I dig into these forgotten corners of how people actually lived every single week. And there is a lot more where this came from. Now, let's get to the part of this story that most people never hear. The reason the outside toilet survived goes well beyond landlords and money. A lot of it came down to pure human stubbornness, and it is genuinely surprising. But first, let's follow the slow, grinding death of the outside toilet across the 20th century because it took forever. In 1918, in the aftermath of the First World War, Britain passed legislation that new houses built for working people should include a bathroom with a hot and cold water supply. A real step forward. But read that carefully. It applied to new houses. All the millions of existing terraces, the ones already packed with families, were left exactly as they were, with the toilet still out in the yard. Laws about new construction do nothing for the house you already live in. So, the outside toilet didn't die. It just stopped being built into the newest homes while it lived on in all the old ones. And there were a lot of old ones. By 1951, according to research into postwar Britain, 8 million homes across the country had been officially declared unfit for human habitation. Of those, 7 million had no hot water and 6 million had no inside toilet. Sit with that number. 6 million homes in 1951 with no indoor toilet. This is after two world wars. This is the era of the automobile and the telephone and the beginning of the television age and 6 million British households were still walking outside to a shed. The country tried to fix it with slum clearance, bulldozing the worst of the old terraces and the backtobacks and moving families into new housing with modern plumbing. But you cannot rehhouse millions of people overnight. The clearances dragged on for decades, street by street, and while they ground forward, families kept living exactly as their grandparents had. which brings us back to that child in Manchester in 1961 [music] and the census that captures this frozen moment in time. That year, nearly 7% of households in England and Wales had no toilet inside or attached to their home. And notice the careful wording there because it hides how common the outside toilet really was. That 7% is only the homes with a completely separate toilet out in the garden or shared down the street. the classic terrace setup where the toilet was attached to the back of the house but you still had to go outside to reach it that counted as having a toilet so it isn't even in the 7% the true number of people going outdoors to use the L was far higher than the statistic admits and it was not spread evenly in some rural districts in 1961 more than half of all homes had no inside or attached toilet whatsoever in one area of Norfolk Mittford and Lnitch the figure reached 59% nearly six in 10 homes outside toilet only. And even 6 years later, the 1,967 house conditions survey found that a quarter of all homes in England and Wales still lacked at least one basic amenity, meaning a bath or a shower, an indoor toilet, a sink or hot water. A quarter of the country in 1967 still missing something we would now consider the absolute minimum. There are people alive and well today, plenty of them, who spent their entire childhood walking outside in the dark and the rain to use the toilet, and the toilet was only half of it. In these same homes, the weekly bath meant dragging a galvanized metal tub in front of the coal fire and filling it by hand with water heated on the stove, one heavy pan at a time. Because filling that tub was so much work, the whole family often shared the same water in turn. The man of the house went first into the clean hot water. then his wife, then the children, one after another, each washing in water that got a little colder and a little grayer as it went. That was not some rare hardship in a far-off century. That was an ordinary Saturday night in a great many British homes, well within living memory. Now, here is the twist that makes this story genuinely strange. The part that goes beyond money and beyond slow bureaucracy and into human psychology. When the councils finally came around with grants, actual money offered to homeowners and landlords to install a modern indoor toilet and bathroom, a remarkable number of people said no. They turned it down. Free help to bring the toilet inside and they refused it. And the reason they gave is the perfect final echo of that old Victorian fear. They thought an indoor toilet was unhygienic. They genuinely believed that having the toilet inside the house near where you cooked and ate and slept was dirty and unhealthy and that the proper clean decent place for it was outside where it had always been. Think about what that reveals about people. The myasma theory had been dead as science for the better part of a century. But the feeling it left behind, that gut level disgust at the idea of a toilet in the home outlived the science by generations. It had stopped being a theory and become an instinct passed down from parent to child. A belief so deep that people would refuse a free upgrade to defend it. This is one of the most stubborn forces in all of human behavior. Once a thing feels normal, once it feels right, we defend it even against our own comfort and even against our own interest. The outside toilet wasn't just built into the houses. By the end, it was built into the people. And when the resistance finally broke, it broke all at once. By the time the last big wave of home improvement grants arrived, the demand became overwhelming. In one Welsh area, so many people applied at once that there were around 3,500 applications in a single constituency in a place where the local builders could physically complete only about 250 a year. The dam that had held for 100 years didn't crack slowly. It burst and the whole country tried to move the toilet indoors at the same time faster than there were hands to do the work. There was also, believe it or not, a strange affection for the outside toilet. And that affection is part of why it clung on so long. In a crowded house full of children, the toilet at the bottom of the yard was often the only door in a person's entire life that they could close and lock behind them. The one place where nobody could follow. Men were famous for vanishing out there with a newspaper for suspiciously long stretches, treating the privy as a private [music] retreat as much as a necessity. In a two up, two down with six people packed inside, half a minute of solitude in a cold brick shed was worth something real. It's a small thing, but it counts because it is one more quiet reason people dragged their feet about giving it up. So, you might assume that's the end of it. The grants went through. The terraces got their indoor bathrooms. The outside toilet finally died. Except it didn't fully die. And this is the last strange turn in the tale. As recently as 2010, it was estimated that around 40,000 homes across the UK still had an outside toilet in use. Not ruins. Working toilets in the yards of people's homes in the 21st century, and the attitude toward them had completely flipped. An outside toilet was once a mark of poverty, the thing the slum clearances existed to erase. But by the 21st century, a well-kept original outside L on a charming period terrace had become a quirky feature that could actually push a home sale price above the local average as long as there was a normal bathroom indoors as well. A generation earlier, families were begging the council to tear these things out. Now, an estate agent will list one as a charming period feature. And those old bylaw terraces, the ones built with the toilet out back because the law and the culture agreed that was the proper place for it, are still standing by the millions today. The bones of this story are all around you in ordinary streets right now. So what do we actually do with all of [music] this? It would be easy to file the outside toilet under primitive history and feel a little superior about our heated tiled indoor bathrooms. But that misses the real lesson buried in here. And the real lesson is about how slowly the world actually changes. We tell ourselves that when a better technology arrives, people simply adopt it. The flush toilet works, so of course, everyone brings it inside. But that's not how it went at all. The plumbing was ready long before the old houses were rebuilt to use it. And even once a house could easily take an indoor toilet, the people inside it often still weren't ready to accept one. A belief about bad air invented by people who were wrong reached out across a hundred years and kept millions of children walking into the frost at night long after everyone knew better. The pipes were the easy part. The plumbing was solved in the 1800s. The hard part, the part that took until living memory was changing what people felt in their gut about where a toilet belonged. The next time you flip on a light in a warm bathroom in the middle of the night, remember that this all of this, the indoor toilet you never think about for even a second, is one of the most recent and most reluctant victories in the entire history of the home. It was not inevitable. People fought it. And if you want to see just how bizarre the hidden logic of the houses we live in can get, there's a whole world of it waiting. Nó đã trải qua một quá trình tiến hóa nghiệt ngã và mỗi giai đoạn đều tệ hơn những gì người ta tưởng.
